analysis.one_liner: Bans union dues or membership requirements as a condition of employment nationwide.
analysis.headline: A bill by Senator Rand Paul, with no cosponsors, to outlaw union security agreements nationwide was read twice, placed on the Senate calendar, and never received a hearing or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would repeal the parts of federal labor law that let employers and unions agree that employees must join the union or pay union fees as a condition of the job. Today 28 states already ban these agreements; the bill would impose that rule on the whole country. Because unions must by law represent every worker in a bargaining unit, the change would let workers benefit from union contracts without paying for them, draining union funds and weakening unions' ability to bargain.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers in the 22 states that still allow union security agreements would no longer have to join a union or pay fees to keep a union-represented job. Employers would gain leverage over wages and working conditions, since unions would have fewer resources to bargain and organize.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Employers and workers who avoid union fees

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the provisions of the National Labor Relations Act and the Railway Labor Act that allow employers and unions to require union membership as a condition of employment, so no worker anywhere could be required to join or pay dues to keep a job.
Extends the rule that 28 states have already adopted — prohibiting compulsory union membership — to the entire country, so workers in the remaining states get the same choice.
Applies only to agreements entered into or renewed after enactment, so existing contracts would keep their union security terms until renewal.

analysis.who_pays: Labor unions would lose the ability to collect dues or fees from workers they are legally required to represent, cutting their revenue and bargaining power. Union-covered workers would eventually feel this through contracts and workplaces with weaker union representation; research generally finds right-to-work states have lower wages and unionization, though the bill's text and summary do not quantify this.

drawbacks.text: Federal law makes the union the exclusive representative for every worker in a bargaining unit, whether or not that worker pays dues; repealing union security agreements creates a free-rider problem where workers receive union-negotiated wages and grievance representation without contributing to the cost.

By cutting off dues in the 22 states that still allow union security agreements, the bill would reduce the resources unions have for bargaining, grievance handling, and organizing, which is the mechanism through which right-to-work laws are associated with weaker union coverage and lower wages for workers.

Supporters of union security agreements argue the agreements are negotiated between the employer and the union, so a federal ban overrides the choice of both private parties, not just the individual worker's.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Individual workers who dislike paying union fees gain a small, direct benefit. The cost falls on union treasuries and, through weaker bargaining, on the unionized workforce as a whole; the two are not comparable in scale, since a union contract covers everyone in the unit while the fee objection applies to some workers. The bill also concentrates a change already adopted in 28 states onto the rest of the country, shifting bargaining power toward employers in the states where unions have been strongest.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, read twice, and placed on the Senate calendar, but no committee ever took it up and no vote ever happened before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Rand Paul introduced the bill on January 10, 2022, and it was read the first time and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under Read the First Time.
On January 18, 2022 it was read a second time and placed on the Senate calendar under General Orders, Calendar No. 244 — a holding spot that does not by itself bring a bill to the floor.
No senator cosponsored the bill, no committee action was ever listed, and the action history ends there; the 117th Congress expired on January 3, 2023, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Labor unions and the workers they represent are better off, because the ability to negotiate union security agreements survived. Employers who would have gained leverage from a weaker union funding base gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Labor unions and workers they represent

for.name: Sen. Rand Paul
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and got it read twice and placed on the Senate calendar, which kept it formally alive but brought it no closer to a vote.

against.name: AFL-CIO and organized labor
against.what_they_did: Opposed national right-to-work legislation as a threat to union funding and collective bargaining; no union support appears anywhere in the bill's record.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, and not a single senator from either party signed on as a cosponsor, so support stayed at one member of the 50-member Republican caucus.

industries.note: Unions would lose the right to collect dues or fees from workers they are legally required to represent in the 22 states without right-to-work laws, cutting their revenue. Weaker union treasuries mean weaker contracts for the workers those unions represent.

With union security agreements banned, unions would represent more workers for free and have fewer resources, tilting bargaining power toward management. The gain to employers comes at the expense of the union-covered workforce's wages and conditions.
